response.sql: WITH ratios AS (SELECT p.SEX AS sex, CAST(l.CPK AS REAL) / l.GPT AS ratio FROM Laboratory AS l JOIN Patient AS p ON p.ID = l.ID), valid AS (SELECT sex, ratio FROM ratios WHERE ratio IS NOT NULL), grp AS (SELECT sex, AVG(ratio) AS avg_ratio FROM valid GROUP BY sex), m1 AS (SELECT AVG(avg_ratio) AS mean1 FROM grp), kept1 AS (SELECT g.sex, g.avg_ratio FROM grp AS g, m1 WHERE g.avg_ratio > m1.mean1), m2 AS (SELECT AVG(avg_ratio) AS mean2 FROM kept1), kept2 AS (SELECT k.avg_ratio, m1.mean1, m2.mean2 FROM kept1 AS k, m1, m2 WHERE k.avg_ratio > m2.mean2) SELECT AVG(avg_ratio) AS avg_of_kept_group_averages, AVG(avg_ratio - mean1) AS avg_excess_over_first_mean, AVG(avg_ratio - mean2) AS avg_excess_over_second_mean FROM kept2;

assumptions.assumption: The database is SQLite (or a engine where division by zero yields NULL). A lab row is treated as having a missing ratio when CPK or GPT is NULL, or when GPT is 0, so those rows are dropped.
Each lab test row is one observation; group averages are plain AVG over test-level ratios, not per-patient averages.
GROUP BY SEX makes '' and NULL each their own group, and both are included in the first mean, as the request specifies.
'Above' means strictly greater than (>) for both threshold comparisons.
'Average amount by which they exceed' means the signed mean of (group average minus threshold) over the remaining groups, not an absolute difference.
CPK and GPT are compared as real-valued division (CAST to REAL), so integer truncation does not alter the ratio.
